hook.text: Order one oh one was placed in May twenty twenty-three, by a customer in Boston. Ten months later, she moved to Austin. Ask the warehouse today which city that order came from, and the answer depends on how her customer row handled the move.

plan.text: Dimensions change, and the model has to keep their history. That's this round: fifteen questions on history and the special dimensions. Nine get worked through, then six quick ones.

scd.text: Question one. How do you preserve history when a dimension attribute changes? With a slowly changing dimension, an SCD. Three classic types.

scd-t1.text: Type one overwrites. Set her city to Austin, and both orders now say Austin, including the one placed in Boston. Its three hundred fifty dollars moved with her.

scd-t2.text: Type two adds a row instead. Boston's version gets an end date, Austin gets a new row, and each order joins to the version true on its date: one oh one in Boston, one oh two in Austin.

scd-t3.text: Type three keeps a previous value column: Austin, and before it Boston. That's one step of history. Move her again, to Denver, and Boston is gone.

scd-end.text: Type two is the standard whenever a report has to stay true to its dates. Type one still has a job: fixing a typo, where the old value was never true.

type2.text: Question two. How does SCD Type two work in practice? Two statements. First, close the current row: its end date becomes the day before the move, and its current flag goes false.

type2-insert.text: Then insert the new version, with a new surrogate key, valid from the day of the move to a far future date, flagged current.

type2-join.text: A fact finds its version by date: the order date falls between valid from and valid to. All twenty-four of the page's orders match exactly one version, because the ranges never overlap and never leave a gap.

type2-load.text: In practice that lookup runs once, at load time, and the fact stores the key it found: order one oh one keeps ten oh one for good. Today's view is just the rows where is current is true.

type0.text: Question three. What is SCD Type zero? A value that never changes once it's written, like the date a customer signed up. Load it once, and ignore whatever the source says later.

type0-run.text: Here a second load sends a different sign-up date, and the insert adds nothing: the first value stands.

type0-mix.text: Types are chosen per column, so one customer row can hold a Type zero sign-up date beside a Type two city.

type46.text: Question four. What are slowly changing dimension types four and six? Type four splits the table. The main dimension keeps only current values, fifteen rows, one per customer, and the history moves to a table of its own: twenty-four rows. Use it when history is large and rarely read.

type6.text: Type six is one, plus two, plus three. It versions rows like Type two, and every row also carries the current value, so order one oh one reports Boston as it was, and Austin as it is now, without a second join.

type6-cost.text: The price: every move rewrites that current column on all of the customer's old rows.

late.text: Question five. How do you handle late-arriving dimension members? Here an order for customer seventy-seven lands before customer seventy-seven does.

late-drop.text: Look up its key with an inner join, and the order simply vanishes: seven hundred dollars loaded, out of eleven hundred ten. No error, just a smaller total.

late-fix.text: Instead, insert a placeholder row for seventy-seven, its city unknown and flagged inferred, and load the order against that key.

late-arrive.text: When the real customer arrives, update the placeholder in place. The order already points at it, so it reports Tulsa, and the fact table is never touched.

late-shared.text: One shared unknown row, key minus one, works too, but then every one of those facts has to be re-keyed later.

snap.text: Question six. What is a snapshot versus insert-only fact table strategy? Insert-only appends a row for every change: six rows for two orders, the whole history.

snap-one.text: A snapshot keeps one row per order, its state now. That's easy to query, but order five oh two just says cancelled. Nothing says it was paid first.

snap-log.text: The log can answer that: five oh two was paid, then cancelled. And it can rebuild the snapshot, by keeping the latest row per order. The snapshot can't rebuild the log.

snap-end.text: So when history has to be auditable, keep the insert-only log as the record, and serve the snapshot from it.

bridge.text: Question seven. What is a bridge table and when do you need one? When one fact relates to several members of a dimension, like an order that used two promotions at once. The fact table only has room for one promotion key.

bridge-pairs.text: So a bridge table sits between them, holding one row per order and promotion pair.

mtm.text: Question eight. How do you model a many-to-many relationship between facts and dimensions? With that bridge, and a weight.

mtm-fan.text: Join through the bridge and sum, and every order counts once per promotion: three orders worth two hundred dollars report three hundred forty.

mtm-weight.text: Give each pair a weight, summing to one per order, multiply before you sum, and the promotions share exactly two hundred.

mtm-end.text: The unweighted totals still say how much revenue each promotion touched. Just never add them up.

vault.text: Question nine. What is a data vault, and when would you choose it over a star schema? A vault splits the model three ways. Hubs hold the business keys. Links hold the relationships between hubs. Satellites hold the descriptive attributes, a new row for every change, stamped with when it loaded and which source sent it.

vault-why.text: Loading only ever inserts, and each source gets its own satellites, so teams add sources in parallel, and every value traces back to where it came from.

vault-when.text: Choose it for many changing sources and strict audit. Choose a star when the domain is stable and analysts query it directly. Often it's both: the vault stores the history, and stars built on top of it serve the reports.

rapid-in.text: The last six are special cases, a sentence or two each.

r-degen.text: A degenerate dimension is a dimension with no table behind it, like an invoice number kept on the fact. You still group by it.

r-junk.text: A junk dimension gathers small flags, payment type, gift or not, web or store, into one table of every combination: twelve rows, and the fact carries one key instead of three.

r-role.text: A role-playing dimension is one table in several roles: the date dimension, joined once as the order date and once as the ship date.

r-mini.text: A mini-dimension moves fast-changing attributes, like age band and income tier, out of a big customer dimension into a small one, twenty rows here, with its own key on the fact. The big one stops growing a new version every time a band changes.

r-factless.text: A factless fact table has no measures at all: one row per event, like a student attending a class. Counting the rows is the measure.

r-uuid.text: And a surrogate key from a sequence is a small integer, handed out in order: compact and quick to join. The other choice is a UUID, a universally unique identifier: sixteen bytes any system can make without a shared counter, which matters when many sources insert at once.

r-uuid-cost.text: The cost shows in the index. In Postgres, a hundred thousand random UUIDs built a primary key index almost twice the size of the sequence's. Time-ordered version seven UUIDs land in between.

next.text: Every table here is filled by a load job: close a version, insert a placeholder, split a weight. Loading the model takes code. Next: Python for data engineering.
